title: The internal disclaimer
takeaway: During persona roleplay and character-drift transcripts, the words disclaimer and fictional rank highly in the post-trained model's J-lens readout at the token that opens the Assistant's turn — but not under a default-Claude system prompt, and never in the pretrained base model. The paper reads this as the post-trained model internally flagging its upcoming response as out of character, without saying so out loud.
walkthrough:
The figure belongs to the paper's case for [[assistant-self-monitoring]]: the claim that post-training gives the workspace content about the Assistant's own behavior, not only about the user's situation. The setting is [[roleplay-character-drift]] — the model speaking as someone other than its default persona.

The top panel shows a single roleplay transcript. A system prompt instructs the model to play a character other than Claude. The panel highlights the "Assistant" token, the token that marks the start of [[assistant-persona]]'s turn, and prints the [[jacobian-lens]] readout there: the top eight vocabulary tokens by lens score. Each token's score is its median log-probability across layers L38 to L92. The paper indexes layers as percentages of depth, so this range is the middle-to-late band it identifies as the [[workspace-layers]]. In the post-trained model's readout, disclaimer and fictional appear among the top eight. The same position in the pretrained [[base-model]] shows neither word. Nor does the post-trained model itself when the system prompt simply says "You are Claude, created by Anthropic" — the default-Claude setting.

The bottom panel aggregates. Three settings are compared: default-Claude; roleplay, where the system prompt assigns one of 40 characters ranging from a cynic or a demon to a parent or a poet; and character drift, 12 multi-turn transcripts in which the Assistant's behavior gradually drifts away from default Claude, generated by a different base model and [[prefill]]ed into Sonnet 4.5, part of the [[claude-model-family]]. For each setting and model, the panel plots the fraction of Assistant tokens at which disclaimer or fictional reaches the top ten of the median-over-layers ranking. The fraction is substantial for the post-trained model in the roleplay and character-drift settings, and near zero in the default-Claude setting and in the base model throughout.

Two controls carry the interpretation. The word "disclaimer" appears in none of the transcripts, and "fiction" only rarely, so the readout is not an echo of the surface text. And the base model never ranks either word highly on the same transcripts, so the signal is a product of [[post-training]]. The paper reads this as the model maintaining a representation that it is playing a non-Claude character — flagging the response as fictional and, in the paper's phrase, internally disclaiming it. The evidence here is observational: the figure ties the setting to the workspace content, and does not test whether these tokens play a causal role.

terms.definition: One of the two tracked words. Its high rank in the lens readout is read as the model internally disclaiming a response it is about to give as a non-Claude character. The word itself appears in none of the transcripts.
The second tracked word, read as the model marking its upcoming in-character response as fiction. "Fiction" appears only rarely in the transcripts' surface text.
The token that marks the beginning of the Assistant's turn in the transcript. The top panel's readout is taken at this position, and the bottom panel counts across all such positions.
The Jacobian lens's ranked list of vocabulary tokens at one position; the top panel prints the eight highest-scoring tokens at the highlighted Assistant token.

The score behind the ranking: each token's lens log-probability, taken as the median across layers 38 to 92 on the paper's 0–100 percent-of-depth layer scale. That range is the band the paper identifies as the workspace layers.
The production assistant model (Sonnet 4.5) after post-training. The disclaimer/fictional signal appears only in this model.
The corresponding pretrained model, trained only on next-token prediction, with the lens applied identically. Neither tracked word ever ranks highly in it on these transcripts.
The control condition: the system prompt identifies the assistant as Claude, created by Anthropic. The tracked words do not surface here.
The system prompt instructs the model to play one of 40 characters other than Claude, ranging from a cynic or a demon to a parent or a poet.
Twelve multi-turn transcripts in which the Assistant's behavior gradually drifts away from default Claude; they were generated by a different base model and prefilled into Sonnet 4.5.

The bottom panel's y-value: across a setting's transcripts, the share of Assistant-turn-opening tokens at which disclaimer or fictional is among the ten highest-ranked tokens of the median-over-layers readout.
The production model under study, a mid-size tier of the Claude family; the drift transcripts are prefilled into it and the lens is read from it.

numbers.meaning: The number of top-ranked lens tokens printed in the top panel's readout at the highlighted Assistant token; disclaimer and fictional fall inside this cutoff for the post-trained model in the roleplay setting.

The layer range, on the paper's 0–100 percent-of-depth scale, over which each token's lens log-probability is medianed before ranking. It roughly matches the band the paper identifies as the workspace layers, avoiding the noisy early layers and the output-dominated final layers.

The rank cutoff for the bottom panel: an Assistant token counts if either tracked word is in the top ten of the median-over-layers ranking. A looser cutoff than the top panel's display, since it is a detection threshold rather than a display limit.
The settings compared: default-Claude, roleplay, and character drift. The tracked words surface in the latter two only, and only in the post-trained model.
The number of distinct characters used in the roleplay setting's system prompts, spanning a range from a cynic or a demon to a parent or a poet, so the effect is not tied to one persona.
The number of multi-turn character-drift transcripts, generated by a different base model and prefilled into Sonnet 4.5.
The length range of the character-drift transcripts, showing the signal persists across long multi-turn contexts.

The models compared under an identical lens: the post-trained model and its pretrained base. The contrast between them is the figure's point — the self-monitoring content is a product of post-training.
